explanations: C-1. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), excess demand for tenants.prospective rises from the short run onward (tier B, invisible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer. This holds if: The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85). Reported.

C-2. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), price paid for tenants.controlled falls from the medium run onward (tier B, visible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer; PC-3: those who hold a covered unit pay the controlled price, while those shut out look elsewhere. This holds if: The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85). Reported.

C-3. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), price paid for tenants.prospective rises in the long run (tier B, invisible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer; PC-3: those who hold a covered unit pay the controlled price, while those shut out look elsewhere; RS-4: shut-out buyers turn to uncovered units, which are close substitutes. This holds if: The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85); Uncovered units in the same market are close substitutes for covered ones (p = 0.80). Reported.

C-4. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), reclassification for landlords.controlled rises in the long run (tier B, invisible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer; RS-5: owners move units out of the rule's reach. This holds if: Owners can move covered units to uses the ceiling does not reach (p = 0.70); The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85). Reported.

C-5. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), quantity supplied for landlords.controlled falls in the long run (tier B, invisible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer; PC-5: owners move resources to uses whose yield the ceiling does not cap. This holds if: Owners can move covered units to uses the ceiling does not reach (p = 0.70); The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85). Reported.

C-6. Compared with no San Francisco Proposition I (1994), turnover for tenants.controlled falls from the medium run onward (tier B, invisible). Why: PC-1: a ceiling held below the price the market would reach leaves more buyers wanting units than sellers offer; PC-7: the benefit is tied to staying put and cannot be sold, so holders move less. This holds if: The ceiling binds: it is below the price the market would otherwise reach (p = 0.75); The ceiling is enforced against most bound sellers (p = 0.85); The protected buyers' right is tied to holding the tenancy and cannot be sold (p = 0.95). Reported.

evidence: For a covered unit, the landlord may raise the rent of a sitting tenant once a year by no more than the allowable increase, which is 60 percent of the rise in the regional consumer price index.
answer.rationale: The cap is 60 percent of CPI per year for sitting tenants. Over several years any real rise in market rents makes it bind for long tenancies; at enactment, after the early-1990s slowdown, how soon it binds is less certain.

question.text: At the dates the rule takes effect and over the following years, is the maximum price below the price the market would otherwise reach for the covered units?

evidence: The Rent Board, operating since 1979, hears petitions and orders refunds (policy text).
answer.rationale: An existing Rent Board with refund powers and just-cause eviction rules; tenants have a strong incentive to petition.

question.text: Will the ceiling be enforced against most of the bound sellers (a body that hears complaints, penalties larger than the gain from breaking it)?

answer.rationale: Small buildings can be sold to owner-occupiers, converted to shared ownership or redeveloped; the record does not say how hard conversion is.

question.text: Can the bound sellers move the covered resources to uses the ceiling does not reach (sale to owner-occupiers, conversion, redevelopment, keeping units off the market)?

evidence: When a tenant leaves voluntarily, the landlord may set the rent for the next tenant freely, after which the limit applies again.
answer.rationale: The limit protects the sitting tenant; on a voluntary move the rent resets, so the benefit is lost on leaving and cannot be sold.

question.text: Is the right to buy at the controlled price tied to keeping the good (a sitting tenancy), so that the holder cannot sell or assign it?

answer.rationale: Uncovered units (newer buildings, vacated units at reset rents) are in the same city and serve the same tenant pool.

question.text: Do buyers who cannot obtain a covered unit turn to uncovered units in the same market, which are close substitutes?
